summary: Fairlight, Prosonix and Offence's C64 demo, second in the C64 demo compo at Datastorm 2013: a western-themed intro, physics-driven ball parts, sphere scrollers and a talking greetings head.
why: Sceners single out the physics parts (the pendulum, the bouncing balls inside a sphere), the Censor-style scrollers, the spoken greetings with a deforming mouth and the humour, with several calling it the strongest demo of the compo.

quote.text: This is the best demo from the compo in many ways, full of wonderful parts and innovative effects.

summary: Thesuper's ZX Spectrum demo, which came second in the Alternative Demo compo at Alternative Party 2011, built around chunky full-screen colour effects and scrolling text.
why: A podium finish at Alternative Party 2011 for a Spectrum demo with a firm communist theme in its greetings and graphics.

summary: Chorus's C64 demo that won the demo compo at Árok 2015, coded by Clarence with graphics by Leon and music by guest DRAX of Maniacs Of Noise, Camelot and Crest.
why: Sceners single out Clarence's code: very smooth movement, a fullscreen AGSP part, extended FLD, sprites in the upper border and a puzzling 4-char-wide sprite trick. Several call it a benchmark tech demo despite its short length.

quote.text: Holy f**k! The most fascinating routines I've seen for ages! Guess I'll have to watch this again and again to figure out how it's done.

summary: A two-disk-side C64 co-op demo by Bonzai, Fairlight, Genesis Project, Censor Design and Offence that won the Oldskool Demo compo at Revision 2019. Its theme is the groups poking fun at each other's trademark parts.
why: Nominated for Best Low-End Production at The Meteoriks 2020. Sceners single out the humour, the friendly 'coopetition' between five groups, the lush graphics and the all-border DYPP scroller.
highlights: music by Laxity, LMan, Magnar, Stinsen

quote.text: Neat effects, lush pixels, groovy tunes, a little bit of fight, and a lot of love for the greatest machine ever to exist.

summary: Trilobit's Atari 2600 demo, coded, drawn and scored by Ilmarque with a story by visy. It came 3rd in the Atari 8-bit demo compo at Silly Venture 2k10.
why: A VCS demo that placed against Atari 8-bit computer entries at Silly Venture, and one of the few on the 2600 to credit a story.

summary: Vanity's 4K intro for the Amstrad CPC, placed 4th in the 4K intro compo at Main 2010. Code by Hicks, graphics by Beb and music by Tom&Jerry.
why: A raycasting engine squeezed into 4K on the CPC, packed with exomizer, from a well-known CPC group.

summary: Razor 1911's C64 4K intro, coded by rez with graphics by Sector 9 and music by Ziphoid, placed third in the Oldskool 4k compo at Revision 2014. A framed pattern effect runs under a Razor logo while a scroller loops.
why: Sceners welcomed Razor 1911 back on the C64 and praised its design, transitions and music for a one-file 4K. Its author has said it was his first release.

quote.text: This is really nice and more so that its only 4k.  The patterns in the middle are really effective.

summary: An Amstrad CPC demo from 1991 by Logon System, coded by Overflow with graphics by Ze Big Boss and music by Jonathan Dunn taken from the game Renegade III.
why: A thin fact sheet, but it's a well-liked early Logon System production from the group's coder Overflow, made outside any compo.

summary: A 32-byte intro for the Atari VCS by SvOlli, with Imp credited for hardware design and soldering. It won the Wild compo at Deadline 2018.
why: A compo winner squeezed into just 32 bytes on one of the most constrained machines around, and the hardware credit suggests the entry went beyond a plain cartridge.
highlights: hardware design and soldering by Imp

summary: Fairlight's war-themed C64 demo that won the C64 demo compo at Big Floppy People 2006, with code, graphics and concept by Hollowman, extra graphics by Jackasser and music by zabutom.
why: Sceners praised how its theme holds from start to finish and how smoothly story and effects flow together, singling out the physics animations, the parallax aeroplanes and zabutom's tune, plus a hidden 'Boten Anna' cover.

quote.text: A demo with a theme that works the whole way from the beginning to the end,  now that is something you don't see every day! Very nice use and selection of effects.

summary: Masters of Electric City's Atari 8-bit demo, coded by bob_er with music by Dhor, which won the Atari 8bit demo compo at Glucholazy 2007. It works in text mode throughout.
why: A compo winner built around text-mode graphics, tagged as such, making it a good pick for anyone interested in what character-based visuals can do on the Atari.

summary: Fairlight and Instinct's C64 demo from Black Birdie 2005, a tribute to the LCP party built around digitised scener portraits, a kaleidoscope-filled vector, raycaster maze, tunnel, twister, chesswaver and an end upscroller.
why: Sceners like its mix of serious code and an unserious, sarcastic attitude, singling out the kaleidoscope, the fast raycaster with Maktone's face jumping out of the maze, and the high-quality end upscroller.

quote.text: This is how a fast production should always be: Good music, nice graphics, sweet sarcasm, serious code and unserious attitude.

summary: Elysium's three-disk-side C64 demo built around a science-lab theme, winner of the demo compo at X 2026. Music by Shogoon, with code from Digger, Brush, MMS, YTM and others, plus a hidden part.
why: Sceners praise its full-border vector work, the haunting big-eye animation, the CRT text effects and Shogoon's soundtrack, and welcome Elysium's return with a demo whose concept runs through every part.

quote.text: the flow, soundtrack, storyline, code, gfx, art direction, polishing, literally everything was 11/10 :)

summary: Agenda's Atari XL/XE demo that won the Atari XL/XE demo compo at Silly Venture 2k19, with code from five coders, graphics by Ooz, Piesiu, Raphis and Ripek, and music by AceMan, Caruso and stRing.
why: A compo winner at Silly Venture 2019 that went on to the Meteoriks 2020 watchlist, made by a large team of Atari 8-bit regulars.

summary: An 8K intro for the ZX Spectrum by T$ Ripoff Institute, with code, music and graphics all by Gasman. Made as a birthday present, it placed third in the combined intro competition at Nordlicht 2014.
why: A one-person 8K production that placed at Nordlicht 2014. It was made as a birthday present, and its tags tie it to Raving Tomatoes.

summary: Panoramic Designs' C64 demo from 1992, shared =7th in the C64 demo compo at Hurricane and Brutal Summer Party. Music comes from several hands, including Ben Daglish, Olav Mørkrid and GT.
why: A long-standing CSDb favourite. Sceners single out the layered parallax, sprites caught between foreground and background effects, the ghost-byte "i" drawn with $d016 alone, the "Blue" and "Home" parts and the speed-changing end scroller.

quote.text: Very thematic, strongly designed, deep and dark and brooding and beautiful...

summary: New Generation's two-disk-side Atari 8-bit demo that came second in the demo compo at QuaST 2004, with code by Solo and Laoo, graphics by Tiger and music by Miker, X-Ray and Solo.
why: A podium finish at QuaST 2004 from a full New Generation line-up, and it is well regarded on Pouët with no thumbs down.

summary: Digital Reality's ZX Spectrum demo from 1996, which placed fourth in the ZX Spectrum demo competition at Enlight 1996.
why: A mid-nineties Spectrum party demo from Digital Reality that held its own at Enlight 1996, finishing fourth in the Spectrum demo compo.

summary: Arise's C64 demo that won the C64 demo compo at Silesia 8 in 2017, with code by Luke, Mojzesh, Wacek and Rodney and music by Jammer. Parts include textured faces, split vectors, glenz marching cubes and an all-border chessboard.
why: Sceners single out its design, syncing and transitions, calling it fresh and stylish. Bitbreaker held it up as proof that good transitions beat storytelling-heavy design, though some found the texture rotator runs long.

quote.text: A good proof that cool transitions work way better than lots of artsy fartsy design that focusses on storytelling only. You hit the sweet spot with this.

summary: Hooy-Program's ZX Spectrum 48K demo that won the ZX Spectrum demo compo at Forever 2014, with parts coded by Gasman, Lvd, TK90X Fan, Ralf, Hellboj and Alone Coder.
why: A first place at Forever 2014, and a collaborative piece pooling six coders and four graphicians, with music by Yerzmyey and Mister Beep across AY and beeper.

summary: Singular Crew's Commodore 64 demo, placed 5th in the Console/Real Wild compo at Breakpoint 2008.
why: A Breakpoint 2008 wild-compo entry from Singular Crew, well received on Pouët. The fact sheet is thin, so it's one to judge for yourself.

summary: A one-file C64 demo by Plush, Instinct and Oxyron, coded by Krill, Jackasser and Graham with music by Fanta. It placed 4th in the demo compo at X 2004 and has hidden parts and an interactive mode.
why: Sceners praise the smooth, polished effects with an oldschool touch, Fanta's atmospheric soundtrack and the transitions. Several also single out JackAsser's debut as a coder.

quote.text: a really nice demo doing a great job combining really smooth effects with an oldschool touch.

summary: Agenda's Atari 8-bit demo from Silly Venture 2k13, where it placed third in the Atari XL/XE demo compo. Code by Probe, music by stRing, graphics by Ooz, Ripek and Piesiu.
why: A podium finish at Silly Venture, the main Atari 8-bit party, with three graphicians credited. That points to a demo built around its artwork.

summary: A C64 demo by Extend and Genesis Project, coded by Elder0010 with graphics by Sulevi and music by psych, that won the demo compo at Transmission64 2025. Its abstract narrative carries an AI-critical message.
why: Nominated for Best Oldschool Production at The Meteoriks 2026. Sceners praise the coherent design from a three-person team, Sulevi's pixel work, psych's soundtrack and the way the parts flow together.

quote.text: There is a mesmerizing flow to the demo, both due to the rhythmic beat of the music, the somewhat abstract narrative that still gets a message through, the unusual color choices, and the awesome effects.

summary: A Commodore 64 demo by Fairlight, Prosonix and Offence that won the C64 demo compo at Datastorm 2018, with music by Ole Marius Pettersen and graphics by Pal.
why: Sceners single out the intricate animations, the helix scroller, Pal's design and OMP's soundtrack, which one commenter called probably his favourite tune from all the Datastorm compos.

quote.text: Beautiful design! Mesmerizing anims and classic soundtrack from Prosonix. The tube scroller looks awesome!

summary: Onslaught's C64 demo marking the group's 20th anniversary, coded by Conjuror and Algorithm with guest artists Yazoo, bizk and ptoing. It won the Oldskool Demo compo at Under Construction 2015.
why: Sceners praise its polish, transitions and soundtrack by Adam and Psycho8580, and single out the rotating pyramid, the twister parts and the circular scroller over the opening fullscreen picture.

quote.text: Highlights for me were the rotating pyramid and the circular "scroller". A splendid soundtrack and gorgeous graphics also helps make this a remarkable release.

summary: A short C64 demo from Oxyron, coded by Axis and Graham with graphics by Yazoo and Oys, that came third in the C64 demo compo at Little Computer People 2009.
why: Sceners single out the fullscreen glenz vector, the mirrored vector and Oys' fullscreen graphics, along with Fanta's Rob Hubbard-style Light Force tune and Kasmo's end music. It is a compact production with a good flow.

quote.text: Wow, I really enjoyed this small piece, nice flow and great tune.

summary: Spirius is a ZX Spectrum demo by mayHem, released at Enlight 1997 where it was entered in the ZX Spectrum demo competition. Code is by Fyrex and Mouze, graphics by Amok and music by Demon.
why: A late-1990s Spectrum demo from the Enlight 1997 compo with a named crew covering code, graphics and music. It's worth a look for the Spectrum demo work of that period.

summary: A ZX Spectrum demo by mr.plop, dr.kvetch and sugar ass m.d., which won the ZX Spectrum demo compo at DiHalt 2010.
why: It took first place in the Spectrum demo competition at DiHalt 2010 and is well liked on Pouët.
highlights: digitised faces beside a big green logo
toilet picture with "I will wait for you at the end"

summary: Agenda's Atari XL/XE demo, which won the demo compo at Lost Party 2026. A large team effort with code by six coders including Ilmenit and xeen, graphics by four artists and music from AceMan, Caruso and stRing.
why: It took first place in the demo competition at Lost Party 2026, and it is a big production for the platform that needs a 320K machine.

summary: A 1987 Commodore 64 cracktro by Eagle Soft Incorporated for their release of Mini Putt, showing the group's eagle logo picture above a scrolling message.
why: A straightforward example of late-1980s C64 cracking-group intros, with a large hand-drawn eagle as the centrepiece.

summary: A 1K intro for the Atari 8-bit by PG and MaPa, placed second in the Atari 1K Intro compo at Forever 2010.
why: A second place in a 1K compo at Forever 2010, packing a scroller-themed show into a kilobyte on the Atari 8-bit.

summary: An Amstrad CPC demo by Mortel and Arkos from 2005, with code, graphics and music by Targhan, Rainbird, Ramlaid and Grim, plus graphics from Beb and Supersly.
why: A joint effort from two CPC groups with a long list of graphics contributors, so the artwork is a large part of the draw. No compo placing is recorded.

summary: Hoaxers' C64 demo for a 512K REU, winner of the Oldskool Demo compo at Solskogen 2015, built around large artwork by Joe and others, with a hires rotator, bitmap movers and scrollers.
why: Sceners single out Joe's huge, detailed graphics and a soundtrack that doesn't sound like typical SID fare. Even those wary of REU demos called it the best of its kind so far, with the hires rotator drawing particular praise.

quote.text: Hires rotator made my jaw stretch way too much

summary: A joint Commodore 64 demo by Atlantis and Padua that won the C64 demo compo at Transmission64 2021. Eight coders and several artists contributed to a run of effect and graphics parts themed around the Unity logo.
why: Nominated for Best Oldschool Production at The Meteoriks 2022. Sceners single out the smooth transitions and flow, the "Japanese sun" hi-res part, the fist part, and the music by Toggle and Mibri.

quote.text: High-spirited and well designed.. great flow and gfx.  Music could not be more suitable.

summary: SHAPE's C64 demo, the party version shown at Little Computer People 2009 where it placed 4th in the C64 demo compo. Code by 6R6, graphics by Archmage, music by GT. The finished Artillery 100% followed in 2010.
why: Sceners single out GT's soundtrack above all, along with the graphics, a Tetris-style screen wipe and a twister with fresh moves. Some noted the reused graphics but still rated it highly.

quote.text: Great graphics, great design and coding execution and a very awesome sound track!

summary: Mahoney's 4K intro for the C64, winner of the C64 4K Intro compo at Datastorm 2017. It runs in an endless loop and carries the message "I belong with those who don't belong".
why: Sceners were surprised by how much fits in 4K, including samples, a sprite mixer effect and glitchy, organic-looking visuals. They also called it original and emotional.

quote.text: One of the highlights from the entire compo. Very original and emotional, crammed down in just 4k.

summary: Tjoppen's 4K intro for the Atari 2600 VCS, which won the Oldskool 4K Intro compo at Revision 2012.
why: A compo winner at Revision on one of the most constrained machines around, coded single-handedly by Tjoppen in 4K.

summary: Ikon Visual's comeback C64 demo, coded and drawn by Munkey with music by Olsen, which won the Oldskool Demo compo at Syntax 2010 with filled 3D vector tunnels and shapes.
why: Sceners welcomed it as the return of Ikon Visual and a rare non-European release, singling out the speed of the effects, the music sync and the octagonal tunnel.

quote.text: Very fun and fast...the octagonal tunnel was a fun ride.

summary: Digital Reality's ZX Spectrum demo from 1997, which placed second in the ZX Spectrum demo compo at Enlight 1997. Code by Flying, Orion and Sauron, graphics by Radio Alex, Terror, Oz and Arty, music by Bloody Joseff.
why: A runner-up at Enlight 1997 from a large Digital Reality team, with credits that include 3D and video graphics by Oz alongside design by Arty.

summary: Oxyron and Crest's Commodore 128 demo, second in the Wild compo at Mekka & Symposium 2001. It comes in two halves, one on the C128's VDC chip and one on the VIC. This video shows the VIC part.
why: It is one of the very few real C128 demos. Sceners single out how colourful it is: Crossbow coaxed new colours out of the VIC with the C128's $d030 bit, and Graham's VDC work is called a milestone.

quote.text: Both VDC and VIC parts are very colourful and great to watch.

summary: Carillon's VIC-20 demo, coded and drawn by Heatbeat with music from Reed, Dizzy and Major Tom, which came third in the Oldskool Demo compo at Assembly 2004.
why: A placing at Assembly's oldskool compo against bigger machines is a fair showing for an unexpanded VIC-20. Worth a look for anyone curious what the smallest Commodore could do in 2004.

summary: A 4K intro for the ZX Spectrum 128K by Darklite and Offence, coded by Neon with graphics by Pal and music by Response. It placed third in the Oldskool Intro compo at Revision 2022.
why: A Revision podium finish in a mixed oldskool intro compo, squeezing a multicolour-mode show into 4K with Shrinkler compression.

summary: LaResistance's 64K intro for the Atari 8-bit, tagged as a remake of an Oxygene production. It came 2nd in the Atari 8-bit Demo compo at Silly Venture 2k10.
why: A podium finish at Silly Venture, the main Atari 8-bit party, with code by Pr0be and Fox, graphics by Ooz and music by Miker.

summary: wAMMA's 4K intro for the Atari VCS, released at Icons 2007 where it placed second in the demo competition. Credits are shown in vertical text between banded colour bars.
why: A second place in the Icons 2007 demo compo, and a 4K production on the Atari 2600 from a team of five, with code by visy, Ilmarque and tatu.

summary: A Commodore PET 8296 demo by Rabenauge, Plush and Crest, with code by Bodo, Krill and Insane. It won the Oldschool Demo compo at Deadline 2025.
why: Besides its Deadline win, it was nominated at The Meteoriks 2026 for both Best Oldschool Production and Outstanding Technical Achievement, which is rare recognition for a PET production.

summary: A 4K intro for the Commodore 64 DTV by Tristar and Red Sector Inc., coded by Benson and Peiselulli with music by Jeff, marking 25 years of Krawall. It came 3rd in the Oldschool Demo compo at Nordlicht 2015.
why: One of the few releases for the C64 DTV joystick-computer, squeezed into 4096 bytes. Sceners praise its fast change of effects and call it worth adding to the flash memory.

quote.text: Great demo for DTV! Fast change of effects.

summary: Dekadence's C64 demo from Stream 2005, where it took second place in the demo compo. Code by BriteLite, music by Intensity.
why: Sceners single out the effects and Intensity's trance soundtrack. They also praise BriteLite's code, from the dithered flexible bar to a clever trick of fitting eight 2x2 pixels into a character.

quote.text: A great soundtrack, exactly my kind of thing. The demo is very good aswell, that dithered flexible bar is my favourite effect

summary: A C64 demo by Tristar and Red Sector Inc., coded by Street Tuff to a tune by Intensity. It placed third in the Alternative Platforms compo at Evoke 2011, up against PC and WebGL entries.
why: Made as a tribute to the late musician Arman (Intensity). Sceners praise the smooth precalculated animations packed into a one-filer, the transitions and the tight sync to the music.

quote.text: Amazingly smooth effects, and all this precalculated animation in a one-filer! I'm impressed. Good sync, too.

summary: New Generation and Zelax's joint Atari 8-bit demo that won the demo compo at Lost Party 2022, with code from five coders, graphics by Tiger and Blasph and music by Tatqoo, Miker and LiSU.
why: First place in the Lost Party 2022 demo competition, and a large collaboration between two groups pooling a big crew of coders, artists and musicians.
